item.title: Voltage Lodge Turns a Historic Collie Building Into an Adventure Base
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
A 90-year-old former co-op storeroom has found a new life in Collie, where Voltage Lodge has opened as a purpose-built accommodation base for travelers exploring Western Australia’s growing adventure scene. Designed for groups, the lodge sleeps up to 30 guests and combines private ensuite rooms with bunk and family accommodations, alongside a communal kitchen and lounge intended to encourage travelers to gather after a day outdoors.

The property is particularly geared toward mountain bikers, with secure storage for up to 30 bikes, e-bike charging, a wash-down bay and repair station. With Collie developing a reputation for its mountain biking and trail network, Voltage Lodge adds accommodation specifically designed around the needs of active travelers while preserving the character of the historic building.

The Curated Take:
There is something compelling about a new hotel that responds directly to the identity of its destination. Voltage Lodge isn’t trying to turn Collie into something it isn’t; it is designed around the forests, trails, rivers and cycling culture that are already drawing visitors there, making the accommodation part of the adventure rather than simply a place to sleep.

item.title: Daytona Beach’s Fall Festival Calendar Celebrates Art, Motorcycles, Cars and Coastal Culture
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
From roaring motorcycles and polished classic cars to juried art, Greek traditions and fresh seafood, the Daytona Beach area is embracing fall with a diverse lineup of festivals and special events. The calendar stretches from October through Thanksgiving weekend, offering visitors multiple ways to experience the destination beyond its famous beaches and motorsports heritage.

The season begins with the 34th annual Biketoberfest®, taking place October 15–18, featuring live music, industry vendors, bike shows, motorcycle racing at Daytona International Speedway and scenic rides along routes such as A1A, Main Street and the Ormond Beach Scenic Loop. November brings the 63rd annual Halifax Art Festival, showcasing more than 200 juried artists along the Halifax River, alongside the Greek Festival at St. Demetrios Greek Orthodox Church, where traditional food, music, dancing and crafts celebrate more than four decades of local heritage. The Riverfest Seafood Festival follows November 21–22 in Ormond Beach, while DeLand’s Fall Festival of the Arts presents 150 juried artists in downtown’s historic setting. Closing out the season is the 53rd annual Daytona Turkey Run, November 25–29, where thousands of classic and custom vehicles, automotive parts and memorabilia take over Daytona International Speedway.

The Curated Take

Daytona Beach’s fall festival season reveals a destination with a broader cultural personality than its racing reputation might suggest. The combination of major enthusiast gatherings, established art festivals, community traditions and waterfront food events creates an appealing mix of experiences, whether visitors arrive for a particular passion or simply want to explore the region at a lively time of year. For travelers, the festival calendar also offers a useful reason to venture beyond the beach and discover the distinct character of Daytona Beach, Ormond Beach and DeLand.

item.title: Australia and New Zealand Renew a Classic Cricket Rivalry in Perth
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Perth’s Optus Stadium will host the opening Test of the Chappell-Hadlee Series when Australia takes on New Zealand from December 9–13, 2026. The match marks the return of the trans-Tasman rivalry to Australian shores and will form part of the series continuing into January 2027. Premium hospitality packages will also be available, including signature dining experiences, private suites and outdoor boxes.

For cricket fans, the fixture offers the chance to see two neighboring nations compete in one of the sport’s most familiar rivalries, while Perth provides a distinctive setting for the opening encounter. The stadium’s hospitality options also position the event as an experience that can appeal to travelers looking to combine live sport with a more elevated spectator setting.

The Curated Take:
A Test match offers a different rhythm from many major sporting events, with time to settle into the atmosphere and let the day unfold. For visitors, the Chappell-Hadlee Series provides an opportunity to experience a classic cricket rivalry while enjoying Perth’s modern stadium and broader destination appeal.

item.title: Pair’d Margaret River Region Brings Global Chefs and Local Wine Together
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Margaret River Region’s celebrated food and wine scene will take center stage during Pair’d Margaret River Region, returning November 19–22, 2026. The four-day festival brings together winemakers, chefs, musicians and producers across some of the region’s most distinctive venues, with a program that includes beachside feasts, cellar-door experiences, intimate meals and events celebrating the area’s acclaimed wines.

This year’s lineup includes Michelin-starred chefs Dave Pynt, Matt Abé and Matt Abergel, alongside renowned American pitmaster Rodney Scott. Their participation adds an international dimension to a festival rooted in Margaret River’s own producers and culinary identity. Alongside the visiting talent, the expanded program features music, new events and returning favorites, inviting visitors to experience the region through its food, wine and sense of place.

The Curated Take:
Pair’d is compelling because it treats food and wine as a way of understanding a destination, not simply as a collection of indulgences. The international chef lineup brings fresh perspectives, but the festival’s real draw is the opportunity to experience those collaborations within Margaret River’s vineyards, coastline and local culinary community.

item.title: Cape to Cape MTB Returns to Margaret River’s World-Class Trails
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Margaret River Region will once again welcome Cape to Cape MTB, Australia’s longest-running and largest four-day mountain biking stage race, from October 14–18, 2026. Covering almost 200 kilometers and approximately 2,500 meters of climbing, the event takes riders across a varied mix of farm tracks and flowing single trails, with daily stages ranging from 34 to 59 kilometers.

What distinguishes the experience is the way cycling is woven into the character of the region. Riders gain access to private trails, pass through wine-country landscapes and finish stages with visits to vineyards and breweries, combining the physical challenge of the race with the food, wine and hospitality for which Margaret River is known. The result is an event that showcases the region as both an adventure destination and a place to linger after the ride.

The Curated Take:
Cape to Cape is an example of an event that makes the landscape central to the experience rather than simply using it as a backdrop. The combination of challenging trails, private access and regional hospitality gives participants a way to experience Margaret River that feels distinctly connected to its terrain and local culture.

item.title: Timeless Waters, Modern Revival
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The revival of European thermalism is one of the most exciting trends in luxury wellness travel today. Recognized collectively as a UNESCO World Heritage site, the Great Spa Towns of Europe offer a seamless blend of grand historic architecture, time-tested water therapies, and modern health science. For centuries, royalty, artists, and world leaders traveled to these elegant enclaves to “take the waters.” Today, a new generation of travelers is returning to these classic destinations, discovering that time-honored mineral springs pair remarkably well with modern preventative health, bio-hacking, and deep stress relief.

Baden-Baden, Germany

A 19th-Century Sanctuary of Thermal Baths

Tucked into the edge of the Black Forest, Baden-Baden earned its reputation as the “summer capital of Europe” during the 19th century, though its thermal springs were first loved by Roman emperors two thousand years ago. The town’s historic spa culture centers around traditional bathhouse rituals, best experienced at the Friedrichsbad. Opened in 1877, this grand, temple-like bathhouse offers a famous 17-step bathing circuit. Guests move through a relaxing sequence of warm dry-air rooms, thermal steam baths, soap-brush massages, and thermal soaking pools of gradually cooler temperatures, finishing wrapped in a warm blanket to let the body fully rest.

High-Tech Longevity and Digital Detox

In contrast to its 19th-century bathing halls, Baden-Baden’s modern wellness scene focuses on high-tech longevity and rest. At luxury wellness retreats like Villa Stéphanie, historic thermal water treatments are paired with state-of-the-art health checks, cellular therapies, and personalized nutrition. To combat digital fatigue, guest rooms feature a clever master switch at the bedside that completely disconnects electricity and Wi-Fi across the suite, allowing for a night of uninterrupted, deep sleep.

Vichy, France

Hydrotherapy and the Imperial Drinking Cure

Known historically as the “Queen of the French Spa Towns,” Vichy became a global capital for wellness under the rule of Napoleon III. Built around natural volcanic springs, Vichy’s classic identity is built on mineral hydrotherapy and gut health. Its most famous traditional treatment is the original Vichy shower, often paired with sipping mineral water directly from the town’s natural springs at the historic Hall des Sources. During the shower, two therapists perform a synchronized four-hand massage while a gentle canopy of warm mineral water flows continuously over the body to boost circulation and calm the nervous system.

Advanced Skin Diagnostics and Microbiome Health

While honoring its historic springs, Vichy’s modern wellness focus has expanded into advanced skin care and microbiome health. At the Vichy Célestins Thermal Spa, mineral water is paired with high-tech skin analysis and custom wellness plans. Specialists use diagnostic tools to assess skin health, then design tailored thermal bath routines, nutrient treatments, and anti-inflammatory diets aimed at balancing both gut and skin health from the inside out.

Karlovy Vary, Czech Republic

Colonnade Strolls and Mineral Mud Wraps

Set in a picturesque Bohemian valley, Karlovy Vary—historically known as Carlsbad—is famous for its pastel colonnades and hot mineral springs. During the 18th and 19th centuries, it was a favorite retreat for figures like Beethoven and Goethe. The heart of Karlovy Vary’s traditional health routine is the mineral drinking cure. Visitors stroll along the grand covered colonnades, sipping warm, mineral-rich spring water from traditional porcelain cups with narrow spouts. This internal routine was historically paired with warm mineral mud wraps using local organic peat to soothe aching joints and muscles.

Cold Therapy and Laser Recovery

Today, Karlovy Vary pairs its warm spring routines with modern recovery techniques. Modern medical spas and historic hotels complement hot mineral baths with whole-body cold therapy, exposing the body to sub-zero temperatures for brief, controlled minutes. This dramatic temperature contrast triggers a powerful release of endorphins, reduces muscle soreness, and speeds up recovery, while gentle laser therapies help revive tired muscles and skin.

Bath, United Kingdom

Ancient Geothermal Soaking in Honey-Stone Settings

As the only city in the United Kingdom built around natural hot springs, Bath’s spa tradition spans more than two thousand years, starting with ancient Celtic rituals and expanding under the Romans. The town’s golden age in the 18th century turned it into a masterpiece of honey-colored stone architecture and high-society culture. The historic highlight here is simple yet transformative: soaking in warm, mineral-dense geothermal waters. Soaking in historic settings like The Cross Bath offers a direct connection to centuries of history while naturally easing joint pain and mental fatigue.

Aquatic Bodywork and Subterranean Sound Therapy

Today, Bath bridges its historic waters with modern mind-body therapies. At luxury hotels like The Gainsborough Bath Spa—the only hotel in the UK with direct access to natural thermal waters—traditional bathing is elevated with underwater bodywork. Guests float weightlessly in warm thermal pools during guided movement sessions, often paired with soothing plant-infused body wraps and subterranean sound-vibration therapy to quiet a busy mind and release deep muscle tension.

The Enduring Appeal of Europe’s Waters

The Great Spa Towns of Europe prove that historic water cures and modern wellness science belong together. By preserving centuries-old mineral springs, grand colonnades, and time-honored bathing rituals alongside modern diagnostics, longevity therapies, and digital detoxes, these four destinations remain the ultimate sanctuaries for wellness travelers. Whether seeking recovery from daily burnout, healthy aging, or an authentic connection to heritage, these historic European towns offer a beautifully balanced escape.

item.title: The Fox Den Brings Boutique Eco Cabins to Western Australia’s Wheatbelt
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
A new boutique accommodation experience is coming to Western Australia’s Wheatbelt, with The Fox Den Mukinbudin welcoming guests from February 2027. Set on a working farm approximately 3.5 hours northeast of Perth, the property will feature premium, fully self-contained studio cabins designed around a slower style of travel, with kitchenettes, bathrooms, in-room laundry and outdoor dining areas with seasonal firepits.

The location also positions The Fox Den as a base for experiencing one of Western Australia’s most spectacular seasonal phenomena: wildflower season. Far from the major tourist centers, the Wheatbelt offers broad landscapes, dramatic skies and a sense of space that appeals to travelers looking to trade a conventional hotel stay for something more connected to place.

The Curated Take:
The Fox Den taps into the kind of small-scale accommodation that can make an under-the-radar region feel like a destination in its own right. The appeal isn’t a long list of amenities, but the opportunity to slow down, sleep beneath dark skies and use a thoughtfully designed base to explore the Wheatbelt’s landscapes and wildflowers.

item.title: Belle Isle: Detroit’s Four-Season Island Escape Without a Passport
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Just minutes from downtown Detroit, Belle Isle offers the feeling of an international getaway without the flights, airport lines or passport. Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the 982-acre island park sits in the Detroit River with views across to Canada, inviting visitors to experience a different side of the city in every season. Summer brings watersports, beach days and outdoor concerts, while fall highlights colorful gardens and riverfront sunsets. Winter transforms the island into a snow-covered retreat, with tropical warmth inside the Anna Scripps Whitcomb Conservatory, and spring brings renewed blooms, museum visits and easy walks or bike rides.

Belle Isle is accessible by car via the MacArthur Bridge, by public transportation, and on foot or by bicycle. Seasonal highlights include kayaking and paddleboarding, the free RiverBlast! concert series, Saturday Socials at Belle Isle Commons, the Garden Party supporting the Belle Isle Conservancy, and the Oudolf Garden’s changing landscape. Visitors can also explore the historic Belle Isle Aquarium, the Dossin Great Lakes Museum and the Belle Isle Nature Center’s Winter Solstice Celebration. Together, the island’s cultural, recreational and natural attractions make it an appealing escape for both Detroit residents and travelers seeking an easy urban reset.

The Curated Take

Belle Isle’s appeal is not simply that it offers something to do close to downtown. Its real draw is the way it changes character throughout the year. One visit might feel like a lakeside summer retreat, another like a botanical escape or a quiet winter landscape. The views toward Canada add an international atmosphere, but the island’s deeper charm lies in its combination of Olmsted-designed scenery, historic architecture, community programming and accessible outdoor recreation. It is a reminder that meaningful travel does not always require going far from home.

item.title: Wallabies and Springboks Bring a Rugby Showdown to Perth
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Perth’s Optus Stadium will host a major international rugby encounter on September 27, 2026, when Australia’s Wallabies face the South African Springboks in a Test match for the Mandela Challenge Plate. The meeting brings two of rugby’s most prominent national teams to Western Australia for a high-profile contest as both sides continue their preparations on the road to the 2027 Rugby World Cup.

Beyond the match itself, the event adds another major international sporting occasion to Perth’s calendar, giving rugby fans an opportunity to experience elite competition in one of Australia’s most striking stadium settings. For visitors planning a trip around live sport, the fixture also offers a natural starting point for exploring Perth’s waterfront, dining and cultural attractions.

The Curated Take:
International sport can be a compelling way to experience a city, particularly when the venue itself is part of the appeal. A Wallabies-Springboks Test gives traveling fans a reason to spend time in Perth while adding a distinctly local chapter to a rivalry familiar to rugby audiences around the world.

item.title: Margaret River’s Open Studios Turns the Region Into a 300-Kilometre Art Trail
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
The Margaret River Region will once again become a destination for art lovers when Margaret River Region Open Studios returns September 12–27, 2026. Australia’s largest open studio event brings together 155 artists across a 300-kilometre creative trail stretching from Busselton to Augusta, inviting visitors into the working spaces where art is made rather than limiting the experience to traditional galleries.

The event offers an unusually personal way to explore the region, with participating artists representing disciplines including painting, pottery, printmaking, millinery, mosaic, woodworking, textiles, illustration and installation art. Studios are located in a range of distinctive settings, giving visitors the opportunity to meet artists, see works in progress and discover the creative communities that shape this corner of Western Australia.

The Curated Take:
Open studio events change the way travelers experience a destination because they make the creative process part of the journey. In Margaret River, the format also encourages visitors to venture beyond familiar wine-country stops, following a trail that connects artists, landscapes and communities across the region.
